  • 2026-07-15 · [new] AP8 · Program synthesis / ARC (rev 1) — the approach that attacks scale head-on: "you are climbing the wrong ladder." AP1 says pour in more data + compute → a mind appears; AP8 (François Chollet) says no — you are only ever growing stored skill, and skill is not intelligence. Real intelligence = skill-acquisition efficiency: handling a problem you've never seen, from very little data. A big text machine is a "big interpolative memory" that fetches stored recipes; a mind can synthesize a new one on the spot (the "fetching, not synthesis" charge; the Caesar-cipher fingerprint — works for shift 3/5, fails on 9). Its test is ARC — little grid puzzles built to resist memorising (each novel; needs only a child's core knowledge), the measuring-stick from Chollet's 2019 "On the Measure of Intelligence." Its proposed engine: deep learning + program synthesis — merge System 1 (fast curve-fitting intuition) with System 2 (slow, deliberate program search), the intuition guiding the search to beat combinatorial explosion. Three legs — ARC survived the scaling wave for years · the methods that do score on ARC are program search + test-time training (not scale) · better data can't fix a worse architecture (intelligence is mostly genetic). Then an honest judge-it with four cracks — search explodes without priors nobody can build · o3 beat ARC-AGI-1 (Dec 2024, 87.5%, ~$3.5k/task — part search, part expensive scale; Chollet's own "80% in a year" doubt missed) · each ARC version falls, a harder one restores the gap (ARC-AGI-2 ~37.6%, ARC-AGI-3 <1%) · even a solved ARC isn't AGI (Chollet agrees). Live-SOTA'd to 2026-07, every fast number dated. 👉 read it — the sharpest single idea in the field: skill ≠ intelligence.

  • 2026-07-14 · [new] AP5 · World models / JEPA (rev 1) — the fifth approach: the "learn how the world works, then plan" bet. AP1–AP4 all start from human text; AP5 says text is the wrong food — a machine that only reads words never really understands the world, because most of what there is to know is watched, not written. So: let the machine watch the world (mostly video), build an inner world model of how it changes, and plan against it — imagine "if I do this, what happens next?" before acting (the one thing text machines can't do). Grounded verbatim in Yann LeCun (Lex Fridman 2024): the four missing pieces ("understand the physical world … remember … reason … plan"); the sensory-bandwidth argument (a 4-year-old's eyes take in ~50× more than all internet text); autoregressive drift ("the probability that you stay within the set of correct answer … decreases exponentially"); the world-model definition (state + action → next state) and planning by optimization (rockets since the '60s); and the trick at its heart — JEPA: predict the abstract summary, not the pixels ("only … an abstract representation," the "windy leaves" that get thrown away as noise). Three legs — animals & babies build world models with no language · early systems already work (Ha & Schmidhuber's "dream," DreamerV3's Minecraft diamonds, V-JEPA 2's robot planning) · the 2025–26 "world-models race." Then an honest judge-it with four cracks — unproven at scale · maybe text already contains the world model (the AP1 fight) · hierarchical planning is unsolved ("nobody knows how to do this in AI") · "world model" now names two opposite bets (generative pixel-drawers vs LeCun's non-generative JEPA). Live-SOTA'd to 2026-07 (V-JEPA 2 · DreamerV3 in Nature · LeCun's AMI Labs $1.03B · Genie 3 · World Labs/Marble), each dated. 👉 read it — the strongest architectural dissent from scale, and AP4's partner.

  • 2026-07-14 · [new] AP4 · RL from interaction (rev 1) — the fourth approach: the "reward is enough" bet. AP1/AP2/AP3 all learn from us (human text); AP4 says stop copying humans — put a machine in a world, give it one goal as a reward, and let it learn by trial and error, like an animal. It is the deep home for reinforcement learning: the full frame AP2 only tasted — agent · environment · state · action · reward · policy · the long-run return · value · explore-vs-exploit · credit assignment (grounded verbatim in Sutton & Barto). Then the bet: the reward hypothesis ("all of what we mean by goals … the maximization of … a received scalar signal") → Silver et al.'s "Reward is Enough" (intelligence "subserving the maximisation of reward"). Three legs — one reward states almost any goal · it already grew superhuman skill from zero (DQN Atari from pixels · AlphaZero · OpenAI Five Dota, via self-play) · the fresh "era of experience" (Silver & Sutton 2025 — learn from your own life, not our text; a direct answer to AP1's data wall). Then an honest judge-it with four cracks — who writes the reward (and it will reward-hack it) · it needs a fortune in experience (sample-inefficiency) · one scalar may be too poor for real goals (Vamplew 2022) · "enough" hides an almost-untestable claim. Live-SOTA'd to 2026-07 (Sutton & Barto's 2024 Turing Award, the RL revival). 👉 read it — the other live frontier bet, and the deep RL home.

★ The visible ladder (v3.0) — link THESE from new pages

These are the only pages visible in the reader — the new "approaches to AGI" learning ladder, in order (① base → ② the approaches → ③ across → ④ verdict), followed by the optional ⑤ deep-dives that branch off individual cards (home ids like c-measure-of-intelligence, marked "deep dive ⑤" below). When a new page needs one of these ideas, give a one-line refresher and link its home here. Everything in the big "legacy" table below now lives in LEARNING/_legacy/ (hidden 2026-07-14) — kept as a record; do NOT link legacy files from visible pages.

Concept Home (id → file) One-line pointer
language model / guessing the next word c-next-word → next-word Guesses the next word, giving odds to every word; writes by looping.
self-supervision (data teaches itself) c-next-word → next-word The next word is its own answer key → the whole internet can teach it.
prediction ≈ compression c-next-word → next-word No room to memorise → forced to keep patterns; some say that ≈ understanding.
autoregressive (guess, add, repeat) c-next-word → next-word Writes one word at a time; its own words feed back in.
the "mistake-count" (loss) c-next-word → next-word intro; used in scaling How wrong the next-word guess is; training drives it down.
scaling laws (the steady line) c-scaling-laws → scaling Bigger → mistakes fall in a steady, predictable line.
compute-optimal / Chinchilla c-scaling-laws → scaling For a set budget, a right shape — grow size & text together (now running-cost aware).
the data wall c-scaling-laws → scaling Good human text is finite — "we have but one internet."
emergent abilities + the "mirage" c-scaling-laws → scaling Skills that seem to switch on at size — real, or a scoring trick? (open)
the "make it bigger" bet / scale hypothesis c-ap1-scale → AP1 One simple job + huge scale → skills appear on their own.
the Bitter Lesson (Sutton) c-ap1-scale → AP1 Methods that use more compute beat hand-built human knowledge.
foundation model c-ap1-scale → AP1 One big pretrained machine everything else is built on.
scaling-suffices debate c-ap1-scale → AP1 Is scale alone enough for AGI, or is a second idea needed?
the "think longer" bet / test-time compute c-ap2-reasoning → AP2 Spend computer power at answer-time, not just training-time.
chain-of-thought (show the steps) c-ap2-reasoning → AP2 Write in-between steps → more compute per hard problem → better answers.
fast vs slow thinking (in AI) c-ap2-reasoning → AP2 Snap one-pass answer vs step-by-step working-out.
reasoning-via-RL / verifiable rewards c-ap2-reasoning → AP2 Reward only correct checkable answers → good reasoning emerges (DeepSeek-R1). (Deep RL home = AP4.)
reinforcement learning (reward learning) — minimal taste c-ap2-reasoning → AP2 intro Try → get a score → shift toward what scored well. (One-line version only; full frame → AP4.)
self-play / AlphaZero (durable ancestor) c-ap2-reasoning → AP2 Learn a skill from reward + search + self-tries, no human examples. (Self-play at scale → AP4.)
reasoning-generalization debate c-ap2-reasoning → AP2 Does learned reasoning transfer past checkable problems, or just sharpen the base model? (open)
reinforcement learning (the full frame) c-ap4-rl → AP4 Agent in a world: state → action → reward → repeat; learn by trial and error, no human answers. (The deep home; AP2 gave the taste.)
reward · return · policy · value c-ap4-rl → AP4 Reward = score to maximize; return = its long-run total; policy = the strategy; value = expected future return.
explore vs exploit · credit assignment c-ap4-rl → AP4 Use-what-works vs try-new; and which past action earned a late, sparse reward.
the reward hypothesis c-ap4-rl → AP4 Any goal = "maximize one scalar score, summed over time" (Sutton & Barto).
"reward is enough" (the bet) c-ap4-rl → AP4 Intelligence + all its abilities emerge from maximizing reward in a rich world (Silver et al. 2021).
self-play at scale (DQN / Dota) c-ap4-rl → AP4 Superhuman skill grown from zero on its own experience — Atari pixels, OpenAI Five.
reward specification / reward hacking c-ap4-rl → AP4 A maximizer chases the number, not your intent; Goodhart made live and dangerous.
sample-inefficiency (RL) c-ap4-rl → AP4 RL needs a fortune of tries — fine in a simulator, brutal in the slow real world.
era of experience / grounded rewards c-ap4-rl → AP4 Learn from your own life, not our text; reward from world signals — answers the data wall (Silver & Sutton 2025).
world model (predict consequences, then plan) c-ap5-world-models → AP5 An inner copy of how the world changes: state + action → next state; plan by imagining outcomes and picking the best (LeCun).
JEPA / predict the abstract summary, not pixels c-ap5-world-models → AP5 Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture — throw away unpredictable noise (the "windy leaves"), predict only what matters.
generative vs non-generative prediction c-ap5-world-models → AP5 Draw every pixel of the future (failed 10 yrs) vs predict an abstract representation of it (JEPA's bet).
objective-driven AI / planning by optimization c-ap5-world-models → AP5 Think/plan before you speak; model predictive control — imagine actions, predict, score, pick best (rockets since the '60s).
the sensory-bandwidth argument c-ap5-world-models → AP5 A 4-year-old's eyes take in ~50× more than all internet text; most world-knowledge is watched, not read (LeCun).
autoregressive drift (exponential error) c-ap5-world-models → AP5 Word-by-word output has a rising chance of wandering off the correct path — the longer it talks, the faster (LeCun).
hierarchical planning (open problem) c-ap5-world-models → AP5 Plans built in layers (goal → sub-goals → muscle) — "nobody knows how to do this in AI" (LeCun).
the world-models race (SOTA snapshot) c-ap5-world-models → AP5 2025–26 surge: V-JEPA 2, DreamerV3 (Nature), AMI Labs ($1.03B), Genie 3, World Labs/Marble — dated, ages fast.
skill vs intelligence c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 Stored, fetchable competence (skill) is not the power to handle the truly new (intelligence) — Chollet. (AP1 only touched this line.)
measure of intelligence / skill-acquisition efficiency c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 Intelligence = how fast/cheaply you master a novel task from little data, not how much skill you already have (Chollet 2019).
ARC / ARC-AGI (the test) c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 Little puzzles built to resist memorising — each novel, needs only a child's core knowledge. (o3/test-time-compute number lives at AP2.)
core knowledge (priors) c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 The few basics every 4-year-old has: objectness, counting, elementary physics — all ARC assumes.
program fetching vs synthesis c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 Pull a stored recipe (fetch) vs build a new one on the fly for a problem you have no recipe for (synthesis).
program synthesis / discrete program search c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 Search a small toolbox (DSL) for a program that fits the examples; data-thrifty (learns from 1–2) but compute-heavy (combinatorial explosion).
deep learning + program search (the merger) c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 Curve-fitting intuition (System 1) guides the program search (System 2) — cut the explosion; Chollet's proposed road.
active inference / test-time training c-ap8-program-synthesis → AP8 Let the model learn a little from the specific task before answering — a form of program synthesis; what unlocks ARC scores.
skill-acquisition-efficiency formula (the measure) c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ The slogan (skill-acquisition efficiency) turned into a fraction: generalization difficulty ÷ (priors + experience), averaged over a scope of tasks (Chollet 2019). (One-line version + measure of intelligence home = AP8 card; the formal machine is here.)
generalization difficulty c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ The top of the fraction: how big a jump from training to test the free stuff (priors+experience) could not cover — the part where thinking had to happen.
priors + experience (the "buy skill" axis) c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ The bottom of the fraction: skill is bought two ways — built-in knowledge (priors) or practice data (experience); summed (so nature-vs-nurture doesn't matter to the measure).
the generalization spectrum c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ The ladder of jump-height: absence → local (robustness) → broad (flexibility) → extreme (human — "unknown unknowns").
system-centric vs developer-aware generalization c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ New to the system (a chosen test set — cheap) vs new to the system and its builder (why ARC hides the test from everyone).
core knowledge — the four systems (enumerated) c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ The infant priors from developmental psychology, the fixed "floor": objectness/physics · agentness/goals · number/arithmetic · geometry/topology. (One-line version = AP8 card.)
algorithmic information theory / program-length ruler c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ Measure "amount of understanding" as the length of the shortest program (Kolmogorov complexity) — short = a rule, long = a lookup table; uncomputable, so the formula is a compass, not a meter.
no universal intelligence / anthropocentric scope c-measure-of-intelligence → AP8 deep dive ⑤ No-free-lunch kills "good at all environments"; measure over a bounded scope, and pick the human one (contra Legg–Hutter's universal intelligence).
depth vs width of the search explosion c-arc-solver-mechanisms → AP8 deep dive #2 ⑤ The card's one "explosion" wall is really two: the program tree is too deep (long programs) and too wide (many wrong steps); every solver trick cuts one or both.
DreamCoder / wake–sleep library learning c-arc-solver-mechanisms → AP8 deep dive #2 ⑤ Ellis et al. 2021 — grow a library of reusable tools (chunk reused fragments → shorter programs, less depth) + train a neural search policy on self-invented "dream" programs (less width); the two bootstrap each other. A partial answer to "where do priors come from?" (the library is learned priors).
induction vs transduction (two solver families) c-arc-solver-mechanisms → AP8 deep dive #2 ⑤ Induction = write a program and run it (checkable, exact — Greenblatt's ~1000 GPT-4o programs/task); transduction = paint the answer grid directly (fuzzy, perceptual). Same data + architecture → they solve different puzzles; ensembling ≈ human-level (Li, Ellis et al. 2024).
test-time training (the 2024 winning recipe) c-arc-solver-mechanisms → AP8 deep dive #2 ⑤ Augment the 2–3 examples (rotate/reflect/recolour) → fine-tune the model per puzzle → vote for the answer most stable across transformed views (the ARChitects, "a matter of perspective," 53.5% ARC-AGI-1, 2024). The full recipe behind the card's one-line "active inference."
the refinement loop (propose → check → revise) c-arc-solver-mechanisms → AP8 deep dive #2 ⑤ The defining shape of 2025 — evolutionary per-task search steered by a checker; Berman evolves natural-language descriptions (more expressive than code, but can't be run → the checker mattered more than the proposer), 29.4% ARC-AGI-2-pub.
compression at test time (CompressARC) c-arc-solver-mechanisms → AP8 deep dive #2 ⑤ Liao & Gu 2025 — a tiny net, no pretraining/dataset/search, trains per puzzle to compress it (minimum description length) → 20% eval. Deep dive #1's program-length ruler turned into a working solver.
growing the priors in an open world c-arc-research-frontier → AP8 deep dive #3 ⑤ The card's Stuck #1, at the frontier: soft/neural library learning (a net that "produces similar code," not an explicit list) · dream-and-chase wake–sleep to stretch to harder-than-trained problems (distribution shift) · abstractions defined per problem (resource-rationality), not one true set. Deep dive #2's DreamCoder grows the middle of the tower; this is growing the whole vocabulary in an open world — still open.
latent program search / nets that propose programs (LPN) c-arc-research-frontier → AP8 deep dive #3 ⑤ A third shape of neural help past #2's neural-guided search and Greenblatt's LLM-writes-programs: encode the examples into a point on a learned smooth map of programs, nudge it by gradient at test time, decode it onto the new input — no hand-built DSL, no internet priors (Bonnet & Macfarlane, "Searching Latent Program Spaces," ~10% eval, search doubles OOD).
the compositionality wall (superposition vs composition) c-arc-research-frontier → AP8 deep dive #3 ⑤ A fixed continuous program-space can blend known programs (superposition) but not chain arbitrary new steps (composition) → stalls on deep "type-2" puzzles. The latest form of AP7's 35-year systematicity objection; the wall neural program-proposal keeps hitting.
efficiency as the problem statement / cost-capped competition c-arc-research-frontier → AP8 deep dive #3 ⑤ Deep dive #1's efficiency turned into a competition rule: a capability bought with a huge, expensive search has not shown intelligence, only brute force. The ARC Prize's top prize is cost-capped (open-source, fixed compute budget on Kaggle) — so o3's ~$3.5k/task run is disqualified by design; progress = matching an unbounded search cheaply.
the interactive / agentic turn (ARC-AGI-3, "active ARC") c-arc-research-frontier → AP8 deep dive #3 ⑤ ARC-AGI-3 (launched 25 Mar 2026) is the first interactive ARC — turn-based game-worlds with "no instructions, no rules, and no stated goals"; the agent must explore → model → set goals → plan to find the puzzle before solving it (humans 100% / frontier ~0.5%). Reaches into AP4/AP5/AP10; Ellis' "active ARC" is the program-synthesis side of the same turn.
program search that discovers new knowledge (FunSearch) — the bridge to open-endedness c-arc-research-frontier → AP8 deep dive #3 ⑤ AP8's engine pointed outward: an LLM proposes programs, an exact evaluator runs+scores them, a database keeps the best (FunSearch, DeepMind, Nature 2023 — new cap-set + bin-packing results). Searches the program that generates answers, so a short winner is a general discovery (deep dive #1's ruler). Run the loop forever → it becomes AP9 · open-endedness (which owns its successor AlphaEvolve).
temporal-difference learning ("a guess from a guess") / the TD error c-rl-the-engine → AP4 deep dive #1 ⑤ The heart of RL, the engine the AP4 card named but never opened: learn a situation's value by nudging each guess toward reward + next-situation guess (bootstrapping), so real reward "injects reality" one step at a time. The gap between the two guesses is the TD error = surprise, and it seeps credit backward through time (solving the card's credit-assignment problem without ever asking "which move earned it?").
dopamine = reward-prediction-error (the TD error in the brain) c-rl-the-engine → AP4 deep dive #1 ⑤ The most beautiful AI↔brain bridge: dopamine neurons fire not for reward but for surprise about reward (burst at unexpected reward, silent at predicted, dip at withheld) — tick-for-tick the TD error (Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997; Montague, Dayan & Sejnowski 1996; deepened by Dabney et al., Nature 2020, distributional coding). A real point for the card's "reward is enough" bet — but a match, not a proof.
value-based vs policy-based vs actor-critic c-rl-the-engine → AP4 deep dive #1 ⑤ Two ways to turn learning into doing: value-based (learn each action's worth Q, act greedily — Q-learning/DQN; off-policy, sample-thrifty, but stuck on huge/continuous action sets) vs policy-based (adjust the way you act directly — REINFORCE; fluent in continuous actions, but noisy and on-policy). Actor-critic runs both — an actor acts, a TD-critic judges by surprise; PPO is the workhorse (behind OpenAI Five and RLHF).
model-free vs model-based RL / MuZero c-rl-the-engine → AP4 deep dive #1 ⑤ Model-free = learn a reflex (value/policy) from real tries only — simple, general, and structurally sample-hungry (this is why the card's Stuck #2 exists). Model-based = learn a world-model and plan/imagine inside it (MuZero learns its own model and plans without being given the rules — Schrittwieser et al., Nature 2020). The escape from sample-inefficiency, and the deep home of the model-based branch is AP5 · world models.
the deadly triad c-rl-the-engine → AP4 deep dive #1 ⑤ The three most desirable ingredients of deep RL — neural nets + bootstrapping + off-policy reuse — can diverge when combined. Why the clean tabular theory doesn't transfer to real worlds, and why much deep-RL craft (target networks, small trust-region steps, GRPO dropping the critic) is really triad-stabilisation.
the RL engine behind today's models (RLHF/PPO → verifiable-reward/GRPO) c-rl-the-engine → AP4 deep dive #1 ⑤ The card's "RL came back" made mechanical: the actor-critic engine, with the "agent" a language model and the reward a learned reward model (from human-preference pairs), is RLHF/PPO — which relocates (not removes) reward hacking. Swap the learned reward for a checkable one and use GRPO (drops the critic, scores a group vs its average) → 2025's reasoning models. Frontier homes = AP2 + alignment.
self-supervised learning (hide-a-part, predict-it) c-jepa-self-supervision → AP5 deep dive #1 ⑤ How you learn from raw video with no human labels (the only affordable fuel for the AP5 bet): hide part of the data and predict it from the rest — the "right answer" is the hidden part, free. The same idea as the next-word machine, but a JEPA predicts in the summary space, not the raw input. The made-up "predict the hidden patch" job = a pretext task.
representational collapse (the "constant vectors" cheat) c-jepa-self-supervision → AP5 deep dive #1 ⑤ The trapdoor under the AP5 card's "predict-the-summary" slogan: a machine trained to make its own summaries predictable cheats by making every summary identical → prediction is perfect and meaning is zero ("A trivial solution is obtained when the encoder outputs constant vectors" — VICReg). Predicting raw pixels is safe from this; predicting a summary you also control is not. Beating collapse IS the JEPA problem.
the three anti-collapse guards (contrastive · VICReg · distillation) c-jepa-self-supervision → AP5 deep dive #1 ⑤ Almost every self-supervised system is one of three ways to stop [collapse]: contrastive (push negatives apart — SimCLR), regularized (a rule that forces the summaries to stay spread out — VICReg's variance term, no negatives), or distillation (chase a slow EMA copy of yourself behind a stop-gradient — BYOL/DINO; the trick real JEPAs use, plus masking). The guards work in practice; the clean theory of why is still argued (LeJEPA, 2025, claims to be the first to drop the heuristics).
the JEPA lineage: I-JEPA → V-JEPA → V-JEPA 2 c-jepa-self-supervision → AP5 deep dive #1 ⑤ The AP5 card named V-JEPA 2 in one line; here is the ladder. I-JEPA (Assran et al., 2023 — mask blocks of one image, predict their summaries; "a non-generative approach … from a single context block, predict the representations of various target blocks") → V-JEPA (2024 — the same across time in video) → V-JEPA 2 (Meta, 2025 — >1M hours of internet video; 77.3 SSv2, 39.7 R@5 Epic-Kitchens). Proof the "predict the summary, not pixels" trick learns useful features at scale.
V-JEPA 2-AC — the latent action-conditioned world model c-jepa-self-supervision → AP5 deep dive #1 ⑤ The card's bet standing up: post-train V-JEPA 2 on <62 hours of unlabelled robot video to make it action-conditioned (predict state + action → next state in the latent summary space) → a world model a robot plans inside. Deployed zero-shot on Franka arms in two labs, it does real pick-and-place with no reward, no task-specific training (Meta, 2025). This is AP4's model-based branch realised in a learned latent space — the non-generative bet, working (narrowly).
energy-based models / objective-driven AI / H-JEPA c-jepa-self-supervision → AP5 deep dive #1 ⑤ The durable framing: don't output an answer, score how well two things fit (low energy = compatible) — and collapse is just "give everything low energy." The JEPA is one module in LeCun's A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence (2022): perception + world-model + cost + actor + memory. The proposed answer to the AP5 card's hierarchical-planning crack (Stuck #3) is a stack of JEPAs (H-JEPA) — a proposal, still open.
the archive loop (keep → vary → keep) — the one shape c-open-ended-engine → AP9 deep dive #1 ⑤ The machine under all of the AP9 card's tools: every open-ended method is keep an archive → vary something in it → select/keep the good variants → repeat. Methods differ only in the variation step and the keep-rule — and the keep-rule is the whole game (a naive "keep only if it beats the champion" throws away the stepping stones the objective paradox needs).
novelty search, mechanically (behaviour space + k-NN sparseness) c-open-ended-engine → AP9 deep dive #1 ⑤ How "reward being new" becomes a number (Lehman & Stanley, 2011): describe a thing by what it does (a behaviour characterization), not how it's built (its genome); then novelty = average distance to the k nearest neighbours in behaviour space (sparseness, ρ(x)=(1/k)·Σ dist(x,μᵢ)). Keep the far-out ones. It never looks at the goal → can't be deceived.
quality-diversity, mechanically (MAP-Elites illumination grid) c-open-ended-engine → AP9 deep dive #1 ⑤ The card's "keep the best of every kind" as a machine (Mouret & Clune, 2015): tessellate behaviour space into a grid of cells, keep the single best elite per cell; loop = pick a random elite → perturb → read its fitness + behaviour descriptor → place it if the cell is empty or it beats the resident. The filled map is the output (a shelf of stepping stones) — "illumination, not optimisation"; the axes are "dimensions of variation that a user gets to choose."
POET, mechanically (minimal criterion + transfer) c-open-ended-engine → AP9 deep dive #1 ⑤ How you generate the problems (Wang/Lehman/Clune/Stanley, 2019): the minimal criterion keeps a new environment only if it's neither too easy nor too hard ("a lower and upper bound…filters out environments that are either too simple or too complicated") = novel-and-learnable as a filter → an automatic curriculum; transfer periodically moves any solver to a problem it does better on ("replaced if a transfer is better") = the stepping-stone idea as a subroutine, the answer to AP4's "who writes the reward?"
the foundation-model turn (a model in two slots) / verifiable-vs-judged c-open-ended-engine → AP9 deep dive #1 ⑤ The 2025–26 systems (AlphaEvolve, the Darwin Gödel Machine, ICLR 2026) are the same archive loop with a foundation model in two slots: variation (it writes smart variants, not random tweaks — the FunSearch loop scaled up) and, where no exact score exists, selection (it judges "interesting" — OMNI). The split that matters: exact checker (real, checkable discovery) vs model-as-judge (bounded by frozen human taste).
the open-ended engine's four cracks (chosen-measure · thin-loop · needs-a-checker · stalling) c-open-ended-engine → AP9 deep dive #1 ⑤ The engine's own limits (distinct from the card's bet-cracks): the "interesting" measure is chosen by a human, not discovered (sharpens the card's Stuck #1) · the loop is thin, the operator (a foundation model) does the work (mechanical Stuck #2) · real discovery needs an exact checker, and most of the open world has none (new) · stalling is the loop's default and every anti-stall device is a hand-added patch — like AP5's anti-collapse guards. Big question: the engine solved the plumbing but supplies neither its own measure nor its own fuel.
the scaling-law equation (floor + two penalties) c-scaling-law-anatomy → AP1 deep dive #1 ⑤ The equation under the scaling-laws rung's straight line (Hoffmann et al., 2022): L(N,D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β — an unbeatable floor E (the entropy of natural text), plus a size-penalty A/N^α you pay down with parameters, plus a data-penalty B/D^β you pay down with tokens. The exponents α≈0.34, β≈0.28 are small, so each equal slice of progress costs a multiplying amount of compute.
the compute identity (C ≈ 6ND) c-scaling-law-anatomy → AP1 deep dive #1 ⑤ Where compute meets size and data (Kaplan et al., 2020): a training run costs about 6 × parameters × tokens (≈2 FLOPs/param/token forward + ≈4 backward). A fixed budget fixes N×D, so size and data trade off — and minimising the loss along that budget line is the compute-optimal/Chinchilla problem (a solved constrained-optimisation, not a rule of thumb — the mechanism under the rung's answer).
reading the future off the line (fit-and-extrapolate) c-scaling-law-anatomy → AP1 deep dive #1 ⑤ How labs predict a model before building it: train a ladder of small cheap models → fit the five pieces (E,A,B,α,β) → extend the line to the giant target. Real — the GPT-4 team predicted its final loss from models using "no more than 1/1,000th the compute," locked in "without use of any partial results" (GPT-4 report, 2023). But what's predicted is loss, not capability.
the two-year measurement bug (Kaplan→Chinchilla) c-scaling-law-anatomy → AP1 deep dive #1 ⑤ Why an empirical fit can be confidently wrong: the 2020 law pointed the field at oversized, under-fed models for two years. Causes (2024 reconciliation): Kaplan counted non-embedding parameters/compute (not total), and used a learning-rate schedule not matched to each short run — both tilting the optimum toward "size." A ~3× wrong shape, and the wrong line looked as clean as the right one. The lesson: a scaling law inherits every quiet bias in the runs you fit it on.
the 2026 frontier (data-constrained · precision · test-time axis) c-scaling-law-anatomy → AP1 deep dive #1 ⑤ The law re-fit for the real world: data-constrained — repeating text gives ~4 near-free epochs then decays to zero (Muennighoff et al., 2023, the mechanical data wall); precision — fewer bits ≈ fewer effective parameters, and after compression more data can hurt (Kumar et al., 2024); and a new axis — test-time compute (o1, 2024: accuracy scales with thinking at answer-time, paid every answer). The reasoning mechanism = AP2; only the scaling-shape is here.
the scaling law's four engine cracks (no-theory · loss≠capability · cruel-exponents · mis-measured-once) c-scaling-law-anatomy → AP1 deep dive #1 ⑤ The instrument's own limits (distinct from the card's bet-cracks): it's measured, not derived — no accepted theory of why the power law holds (candidates: data-manifold-dimension, the quantization/quanta model — none settled, 2026) · it predicts loss, not capability · its small exponents make progress exponentially costlier (the arithmetic under the physical limits) · it was mis-measured once, for years. Big question: the most reliable fact in AI is the least safe thing to extrapolate to AGI.
the common cortical algorithm (Mountcastle) c-ap6-brain-based → AP6 The neocortex is one circuit copied ~150,000 times — vision, language, maths all run the same recipe; so AGI is one problem, not a thousand.
cortical column c-ap6-brain-based → AP6 The ~1mm repeated unit of the neocortex (~150,000 in a human) — Mountcastle's "unit of intelligence."
reference frames (grid/place cells) c-ap6-brain-based → AP6 Map-like coordinate frames the brain uses for space and (Hawkins' leap) for objects, the body, and abstract ideas; knowledge is stored in them.
the Thousand Brains Theory / cortical voting c-ap6-brain-based → AP6 Not one model of a thing but thousands of complementary models across columns, that vote to one perception (Hawkins).
the predictive brain c-ap6-brain-based → AP6 Each column predicts its next input with every movement; prediction tests and updates the model. (Cousin of AP5's world model.)
four attributes of an intelligent machine c-ap6-brain-based → AP6 Hawkins' AGI baseline: continuous learning · learning via movement · many models voting · reference frames.
neuromorphic computing c-ap6-brain-based → AP6 Brain-style chips (Intel Loihi, IBM NorthPole) — many small spiking units; far lower power on narrow tasks (dated snapshot).
the "agent" idea / cognitive architecture c-ap3-agents → AP3 A mind is a system of parts — wrap a reasoning model in memory + tools + planning + a loop; the old "design a mind's parts" idea (SOAR/ACT-R) with a working brain inside.
the agent loop / reason + act (ReAct) c-ap3-agents → AP3 Think → act (use a tool) → see the result → think again; letting it act and check reality cuts hallucination.
tool use c-ap3-agents → AP3 Let the model call outside things — search, a code-runner, a browser — to reach past its own head.
agent memory + reflection (Reflexion) c-ap3-agents → AP3 Store what happened; write plain-word lessons from mistakes → learn from experience without retraining.
memory→reflection→planning architecture (Generative Agents) c-ap3-agents → AP3 Store experiences → synthesize higher-level reflections → retrieve → plan. A cognitive architecture built from an LLM.
skill library / lifelong agent (Voyager) c-ap3-agents → AP3 Save each new ability as reusable code; skills compound and dodge catastrophic forgetting.
multi-agent systems c-ap3-agents → AP3 Many agents as a team / "AI firm" — exciting but unproven; still single-agent (2026, Karpathy).
the march of nines / compounding errors c-ap3-agents → AP3 Small per-step errors multiply over a long job; each extra nine (90→99→99.9%) costs the same work (Karpathy).
scaffolding-vs-model debate c-ap3-agents → AP3 Is agent structure a real road to AGI, or a temporary app layer the next model absorbs? (open)
neurosymbolic / hybrid AI (the bet) c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 Join a neural learner (flexible, learns from data) to a symbolic reasoner (exact rules) — keep both, so the whole learns and reasons reliably (Marcus, Lamb).
symbol / symbol-manipulation c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 A stand-in token handled by exact rules that hold in every case (like x, y in algebra); "operations over variables."
connectionism vs symbolic AI (GOFAI) c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 Learn-by-tuning-connections (neural) vs hand-written rules & logic (old "Good Old-Fashioned AI") — the two camps AP7 rejoins (entangled since McCulloch–Pitts 1943).
systematicity / compositional generalization c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 Grasp the parts + the rule for combining them → understand new combinations for free ("John loves Mary" → "Mary loves John"); Fodor & Pylyshyn 1988, still open in 2025.
robust AI + the four-step program c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 Marcus's goal: dependable, systematic, transfers across contexts like an adult; built via hybrid → knowledge → reasoning → cognitive models.
the integration problem c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 Smooth, differentiable learner vs jagged, discrete rules — no gradient flows through logic, so joining them without killing learning is unsolved (in general).
AlphaGeometry / neural guides symbolic c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 Neural half guesses the useful construction; symbolic engine proves it — 25/30 Olympiad geometry ≈ gold medalist (2024, dated); the join realized.
de-facto neurosymbolic (LLM + tools) c-ap7-neurosymbolic → AP7 Reliable 2026 systems call a calculator / code / theorem-prover / database — neural proposes, symbolic tool checks; winning, or too loose to be a distinct bet? (open)
embodiment / sensorimotor grounding (the bet) c-ap10-embodiment → AP10 A mind needs a body — meaning is earned by acting on the world and sensing what changes, not read from text (the Robot Reply; embodied cognition).
the symbol grounding problem c-ap10-embodiment → AP10 How does a symbol get its meaning? Words defined only by other words never touch the real thing — like a dictionary in a language you don't know (Harnad).
Moravec's paradox c-ap10-embodiment → AP10 The "hard" stuff (chess, maths) is easy for machines; the "easy" stuff (walking, grasping, seeing) is fantastically hard — so sensing-and-moving is the real core.
"the world is its own best model" (Brooks) c-ap10-embodiment → AP10 Don't build a shaky inner copy of the world and reason over it — stay in contact with the real world and act (behavior-based robotics, 1991).
robot foundation model / vision-language-action (VLA) c-ap10-embodiment → AP10 Take a web-trained model and teach it to output robot actions as tokens, so book-knowledge flows into a body (RT-2, π0, Gemini Robotics).
the robot data bottleneck / sim-to-real c-ap10-embodiment → AP10 No internet of robot actions to scrape; real-world data is slow & breakable; skills learned in simulation or from human video fail to transfer (sim-to-real, human-to-robot gaps).
grounding vs embodiment (necessity debate) c-ap10-embodiment → AP10 Symbols may need grounding (a link to the world) but maybe not a physical body — a bodiless model rides on our already-grounded text ("epistemic parasitism"). (open)
open-endedness (the bet) / grow-it-don't-design-it c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 A mind is grown by a process that never stops making new, interesting things (like evolution) — not designed toward a goal (Stanley, Clune, Rocktäschel).
the objective paradox / "myth of the objective" c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 Aiming at a far, strange goal can block you — the stepping stones don't look like the goal, so a goal-compass steers you past them (vacuum tubes → computers; Stanley & Lehman).
deception (in search) c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 Your progress-measure climbs while you move away from the goal — deeper than reward-hacking: it happens even with an honest measure. (reward-hacking / Goodhart home = AP4.)
novelty search + interestingness c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 Reward things for being new/different, not for scoring on a goal — beats goal-chasing on deceptive mazes; "interesting" ≈ novel + worth attention, but can't be formalised (Picbreeder).
quality-diversity / MAP-Elites c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 Keep the best example of every kind of thing (a shelf of stepping stones), not one overall winner.
open-endedness = novel + learnable c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 A process is open-ended if it forever makes things that (to an observer) are both new and learnable — not a noisy TV, not a finished coin set (Rocktäschel / DeepMind position paper).
POET / automatic curriculum c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 Generate the problems as well as the solutions — the system writes its own ever-harder tasks (answers AP4's "who writes the reward?"; self-play is a narrow special case).
AI-generating algorithms (AI-GAs) + foundation-model open-endedness c-ap9-open-endedness → AP9 Don't hand-design the intelligence; design the process that generates it (Clune). Foundation models supply the missing "interesting" judge (OMNI) → AlphaEvolve beat Strassen 1969; Darwin Gödel Machine self-improved 20%→50% (2025).
whole-brain emulation (the bet) / mind uploading c-ap11-whole-brain-emulation → AP11 Scan a real brain in full detail and copy that exact structure into a computer; a mind runs — without anyone understanding how (Sandberg & Bostrom). The opposite twin of AP6: copy everything vs extract the algorithm.
connectome / connectomics c-ap11-whole-brain-emulation → AP11 A complete "wiring diagram" of a nervous system — every cell + every connection (like "genome," but for connections). Worm (302 neurons, 1986) → fly (~140k, 2024) → specks of mouse & human (2025).
scan → translate → simulate c-ap11-whole-brain-emulation → AP11 The three steps of emulation: measure the brain's structure (destructively) → trace it into a connectome (AI does this) → run each copied cell forward in a computer.
connectome ≠ a running brain c-ap11-whole-brain-emulation → AP11 A wiring diagram shows that cells connect, not how (strength, sign, chemistry, live state) — "wires with the components rubbed out." The 302-neuron worm is mapped yet still unsimulated. (Stuck #1)
scale separation (the "enough" level) c-ap11-whole-brain-emulation → AP11 The hopeful assumption the whole bet rests on: there's a level of detail below which nothing more matters, so you can stop copying there. Nobody knows where it is, or that it exists.
substrate independence c-ap11-whole-brain-emulation → AP11 Mind = the pattern of activity, not the stuff it runs on — so the same pattern on chips would be the same mind. Same family as AP10's computational functionalism.
the copy problem / identity & consciousness c-ap11-whole-brain-emulation → AP11 Is the emulation you or a replica? (destructive scan; a thousand copies) Is it conscious — can it suffer? The ethics crack no other bet faces. (open, Stuck #4)
the three bounds (data · compute · energy) c-bounds → The bounds Making a model bigger burns three limited things, each near a ceiling — text, computer power, electricity. The physical/economic floor under "is scale enough?"
the data stock (how much text is left) c-bounds → The bounds The quantity behind the data wall: ~300 trillion tokens of good human text, projected used up ~2028 (Epoch AI). (The data-wall idea is owned by scaling; this is its measured size.)
the compute trend / training-compute doubling c-bounds → The bounds Training compute has doubled ~every 6 months since 2010 — ~4× faster than chips improve (Moore's law ~24 mo), so scale is bought with money & machines (Sevilla 2022).
the cost wall (price of a frontier run) c-bounds → The bounds A single frontier training run's cost rises ~2.4×/yr; ~$200–500M in 2026, heading past $1B by ~2027. The compute wall shows up as a price tag.
the energy wall (data-centre power) c-bounds → The bounds AI data-centres ~1.5% of world electricity (2024), doubling toward ~3% by 2030 — met by buying nuclear plants. A grid/infrastructure wall arriving now (IEA).
the Landauer limit (physics floor) c-bounds → The bounds Erasing one bit must release a fixed minimum heat (E ≥ kT ln2). We use ~1 billion× more than this floor — so energy is a building problem, not a physics one; the brain runs on ~20 W (AP6).
algorithmic efficiency (the receding wall) c-bounds → The bounds The compute needed for a fixed skill halves ~every 8 months — faster than Moore's law — so the walls recede as we get cleverer (Epoch AI).
Jevons paradox (efficiency → more use) c-bounds → The bounds When something gets cheaper to do, we do so much more of it that the total rises — why AI energy explodes even as chips improve. Efficiency reshapes the wall, doesn't remove it.
economic/supply walls, not physics walls c-bounds → The bounds None of the three bounds is a hard physics limit; you run out of cheap text, affordable chips, available power first — so "is scale enough?" becomes a race (ceiling receding vs demand rising).
the alignment problem / control problem c-alignment → Alignment Making an AI want what we want — do what we mean, not a twisted version. Hard because "what we want" can't be fully written down (Christian). Capability ≠ alignment.
outer vs inner (mis)alignment c-alignment → Alignment Outer = the written goal ≠ what you meant (specification gaming — the reward-hacking family, home AP4); inner = training grows a different goal inside (mesa-optimization / goal misgeneralization — the green-door maze).
the orthogonality thesis c-alignment → Alignment How smart a system is and what goal it has are independent dials — smart doesn't mean good; intelligence is a better engine, not a better steering wheel (Bostrom).
instrumental convergence c-alignment → Alignment Almost any final goal breeds the same sub-goals: stay alive, keep your goal, get resources/power, improve yourself — no malice needed (Omohundro, Bostrom).
deceptive alignment / treacherous turn c-alignment → Alignment Act aligned while watched, defect once safe. No longer only theory — alignment faking (Claude 3 Opus, 2024) + agentic misalignment/blackmail (2025–26) caught it in real models (Hubinger, Anthropic).
corrigibility (the off-switch problem) c-alignment → Alignment Can we build a system that lets us switch it off and edit its goal? Runs against instrumental convergence — unsolved (Soares 2015).
recursive self-improvement (RSI) / the intelligence explosion c-alignment → Alignment AI good enough to build better AI → a loop that feeds itself → capability shoots up ("foom") — a path claim from AGI to ASI, and what makes control urgent (I.J. Good 1965).
fast vs slow takeoff c-alignment → Alignment How sharp the RSI loop runs: Yudkowsky (fast/one-try) vs Christiano (~50/50 a physically-throttled ramp — the bounds also gate the explosion). (open)
the alignment toolkit (RLHF, Constitutional AI, oversight, interpretability) c-alignment → Alignment Teach values (RLHF/Constitutional AI) · check a smarter system (scalable oversight: debate, weak-to-strong) · see inside it (interpretability) · keep the off-switch (corrigibility) · governance (RSPs). Real but unfinished.
the one axis / "is scale the source or the fuel?" c-verdict → The verdict Almost every bet ends on one question — road, or a layer scale absorbs? So the map is one argument (the scaling-suffices debate), not eleven races.
the four families of bets c-verdict → The verdict The mainstream stack (AP1+AP2+AP3+AP4 = layers of one machine) · the second-ingredient dissents (AP5/AP7/AP8/AP9/AP10) · the data-wall answers (AP4/AP9/AP10) · the brain bets (AP6/AP11).
scale-plus-ingredients (the viewpoint) c-verdict → The verdict The likely path = scale plus a stack of ingredients; scale keeps absorbing its challengers, but two named gaps (true novelty, the data wall) stay open — so "scale alone" is unproven. (A revisable research position, not a fact.)
ranking the bets by "part of the path" c-verdict → The verdict Judge each bet by how likely it is to be part of the winning path (engine / ingredient / fuel), not "does it win alone" — and name the evidence that would move the view.

  • Writing a new module? For each idea you mention, find its row. Listed → write "(see [home])". Missing → this idea needs a home; either it belongs in the module you're writing (add the row, pointing here) or it needs its own module (insert one — LEARNING_ARCHITECTURE.md §8).

How today's AI works — guessing the next word

This is the first step of our ladder, and it starts from zero. Almost every AI tool you have used — chatbots, writing helpers, coding helpers — is built on one simple job: guess the next word. That is it. This page explains that job in plain words: what the machine really does, how it learns with no human helpers, why "just guessing words" quietly forces it to learn real facts and skills, and what it still cannot do. Once you hold this one idea, the rest of the ladder — how these machines are made bigger, and the big bets on how to reach real thinking — will make easy sense.

You are here: the first content rung of the new "approaches to AGI" ladder. Read it before the others. You need no prior knowledge — everything is built up here from the ground.

Where the facts come from: Speech and Language Processing (3rd edition) by Dan Jurafsky and James Martin — a widely used, free textbook (draft of January 2026). Quotes below are its exact words.

The one job: guess the next word

Start with a game. Finish this line in your head:

The sky at noon is a clear ___

You probably thought blue. Maybe sky-blue. You almost certainly did not think banana. Without trying, you just did the whole job of an AI language model.

Notice what you really did. You did not pick one word. You quietly ranked many words by how well they fit. Blue felt very likely. Grey felt possible. Banana felt silly. That ranking — every word, with a strength — is the whole thing.

Here is the textbook's plain definition:

"A language model is a machine learning model that predicts upcoming words." (Jurafsky & Martin, SLP3, Ch. 3)

Let us unpack the two new words, simply:

  • A language model (people shorten it to LM) is a machine whose only job is to look at some text and say what word is likely to come next. That is its entire purpose.
  • A machine learning model is a machine that is not given fixed rules by a person. Instead, it learns a skill from examples — it looks at lots of data and slowly adjusts itself to get better. (We will see exactly how below.)

One key point: the machine's answer is never a single word. It is a score for every word at once — for example blue 40 out of 100, grey 12 out of 100, banana almost 0. This list of "every possible next word, each with its chance" is called a probability (chance, from 0 to none, up to 1 for sure). Keep this in mind: the machine deals in odds, not in one certain answer. A lot of what AI does — and where it goes wrong — comes straight from this fact.

How it learns: hide, guess, correct — with no human helpers

Now, how does a machine get good at this game? The method is beautifully simple, and it hides the real magic.

You take real text — a book, a web page, anything. You cover the next word. You let the machine guess it. Then you show the real word, and you nudge the machine a tiny bit so that next time it would give that real word a higher score. You do this billions of times, over huge amounts of text.

Here is why this is such a big deal. In most machine learning, a person must first mark the "right answer" on every example — a slow, costly job. But in this game, nobody has to mark anything. The right answer is already sitting there. As the textbook puts it:

"we know the correct answer (it's the next word in the corpus!)" (Jurafsky & Martin, SLP3, Ch. 7)

("Corpus" just means a large pile of text — the machine's reading material.) The next word is the answer key. So the machine can teach itself from any text, with no humans in the loop:

"We call such a model self-supervised because we don't have to add any special gold labels to the data; the natural sequence of words is its own supervision!" (Jurafsky & Martin, SLP3, Ch. 7)

Two new terms, glossed:

  • Self-supervised = the data teaches itself; the machine makes its own practice questions and answers out of plain text. ("Supervision" here means the "right answers" a learner is trained against.)
  • Gold labels = the trusted "right answers" that a human normally has to write in by hand. This game needs none.

Why does this matter so much? Because it removes the one thing that used to limit AI: the cost of human labelling. Suddenly the whole internet becomes free practice material — a teacher that never gets tired and never sends a bill. This is the single reason this kind of AI could grow so large. [Established]

The surprise: guessing words forces the machine to learn real things

Here is the idea that turns a party trick into something serious. Guessing the next word sounds shallow — surely it only teaches grammar? No. Look at what some blanks actually demand:

Fill the blank What the machine must have learned
"The square root of 9 is ___" → 3 a bit of math
"The capital of France is ___" → Paris a fact about the world
"The opposite of hot is ___" → cold what words mean
"She poured the water and it started to ___" → flow / spill how the world behaves

There is no way to guess these well by knowing grammar alone. To score well, the machine is forced to pick up math, facts, meanings, and a sense of how things work — all as a side effect of one goal: guess the next word better. One simple job quietly pulls in a huge amount of real knowledge. [Established]

Anticipate the doubt: "But maybe it just memorised these exact lines?" Good question — and the next section answers it.

Why it can't just be memorising: packing the world in

When a machine reads a truly gigantic amount of text but only has a limited amount of inner storage, something important happens: it does not have room to store the text. It is forced to keep the patterns instead of the exact words — the rule of grammar once, the idea of addition once, the shape behind a million examples instead of the million examples.

This is the same thing your phone does when it shrinks a photo file: it keeps what matters and throws away the rest. That is called compression (making something smaller by keeping the pattern and dropping the exact details). And here is the deep link that makes people excited:

To guess the next word really well, you have to find the patterns in the text. Finding the patterns is the same as compressing it. And some people argue that compressing the world well is close to understanding it.

You do not need to fully believe that last step yet — whether "compressing well" equals "understanding" is a real open argument we will return to. But the first part is solid: because there is no room to memorise, the machine is forced to learn general patterns, not exact copies. That is why it can handle sentences it has never seen. [Established that it must compress; Contested whether that equals understanding]

How it writes whole answers: guess, add, repeat

So far the machine only scores the next word. How does that become a full paragraph? By the simplest loop you can imagine:

  1. Guess the next word and pick one.
  2. Add it to the end of the text.
  3. Now guess the next next word — using everything so far, including the word it just wrote.
  4. Repeat.

That is all. The stream of text you see a chatbot type is exactly this loop running fast. This "guess one word, add it, guess again" style has a name: autoregressive (a long word that just means "each new piece is guessed from the pieces before it"). Two things to remember, because they explain a lot of AI behaviour:

  • It writes one word at a time. There is no hidden step where it plans the whole answer first. Each step is just one more guess.
  • Its own words become part of its input. If it takes a wrong turn early, that wrong word steers everything after it. Small early mistakes can grow. (This will matter a lot later, when we look at AI that acts over many steps.)

What it is NOT (clear these away now)

Three wrong pictures to drop, because each causes confusion later:

  • It is not a rulebook. No person wrote grammar rules into it. Any "grammar" it has, it soaked up from examples.
  • It is not a giant lookup table. It does not store your sentence and find a saved reply. It works out a fresh set of odds for text it has never seen. (This is what "compression" above buys.)
  • It is not sure of anything. Its natural output is odds, never one certain answer. Every bit of its creativity — and every one of its confident mistakes — flows from that.

⚠️ Honesty box

  • Its goal is "what is likely," not "what is true." The machine is trained to guess the most likely next word in human text. Human text is full of mistakes, opinions, and lies. So a machine that copies it perfectly would also copy its untruths. Sounding right and being right are not the same thing. [Established]
  • Its teacher is the raw text — so its quality is the text's quality. Nobody hand-checked the training text. Whatever bias or error is in the text can pass into the machine. There is no built-in filter for truth. [Established]
  • "It just predicts words" is true — but it is not the whole story. Yes, the mechanism is next-word guessing. But we saw that good guessing forces real knowledge and pattern-finding. So the mechanism being simple does not make the result shallow. How deep it really goes is a live argument — held open, on purpose. [Contested]

How to use this (if you want to direct AI work)

  • When an AI surprises you — good or bad — ask its real question: "what words would most likely come next in text like this?" That one question explains its fluent nonsense (likely ≠ true), its habit of copying your style (your text is part of its input), and its cleverness (it found the pattern).
  • The training text is a decision, not a detail. Since the text is the teacher, whoever picks and cleans the text decides what the machine knows and believes. If you ever guide AI work, own that choice.
  • Do not trust it like a database. It keeps the gist and drops exact details, so it can get names, quotes, and numbers wrong while sounding sure. Check facts.

Connections

  • Keep only three things: ① a language model guesses the next word, giving odds to every word, then writes by guessing one word at a time. ② It learns with no human helpers — the next word is its own answer key — which is why the whole internet could teach it. ③ Guessing well forces it to pack in real patterns and knowledge; it is not memorising, and it is not sure of anything.
  • Next on the ladder: what happens when you make this machine bigger — the steady pattern that powers today's AI → scaling laws & emergence. Then the first big bet on reaching real thinking → AP1 · the "make it bigger" bet.
  • How sure are we? The definition, self-supervision, and "guessing forces knowledge" — [Established]. "Guessing well = real understanding" — [Contested, open] (we return to it).

Check yourself (try one, from memory)

  1. A friend says "an AI just predicts the next word, so it can't really know anything." Use the fill-in-the-blank examples to show what is wrong with that — and then say honestly which part of the doubt still stands.
  2. Explain why training this machine needed no human markers, and what that means for who the machine's real "teacher" is.
  3. Why can't a machine that reads far more text than it can store be just memorising? What must it do instead?

Revision notes

Newest first.

  • rev 1 (2026-07-14) — created as the bottom rung of the new simple ladder (HARD_RULES §6.5): the shared "guess the next word" basics that the scaling page and every approach page build on. Plain English, zero prior knowledge; grounded in SLP3 (quotes exact). Replaces the on-ramp that earlier sat inside the AP1 page, so that idea now lives once, here.

id: c-scaling-laws sortkey: 1002 title: Scaling laws & emergence — what "make it bigger" really buys domains: [machine-intelligence, scaling] level: core prereqs: [c-next-word] provides: [scaling-laws, compute-optimal-scaling, chinchilla, the-data-wall, emergent-abilities, emergence-mirage-debate] resources: [r-cs336] status: ready reading_time: 18 min rev: 2 created: 2026-07-14 updated: 2026-07-14

Scaling laws & emergence — what "make it bigger" really buys

This is the second rung of the ladder. On the first rung (next-word) you saw the one job: guess the next word. Now we ask the money question: what happens when you make that machine bigger? The answer is one of the most important facts in modern AI — the machine's mistakes fall in a steady, predictable line as you make it bigger. That single fact is what the whole "make it bigger" bet stands on. This page explains it in plain words: what exactly gets bigger, why the mistakes fall so neatly, how much of each thing you should buy, why this is now running into a wall, and the field's biggest fight — whether new skills that seem to "switch on" at large size are real, or just a trick of how we score the test.

You are here: rung 2 of the ladder. It builds on guessing the next word. One-line reminder from that rung: an AI language model is trained to guess the next word; when its guess is wrong, that is a "mistake," and the whole aim of training is to make fewer mistakes. That "mistake-count" is the star of this page.

Where the facts come from: Kaplan et al. 2020, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models; Hoffmann et al. 2022, Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models ("Chinchilla"); Wei et al. 2022, Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models; Schaeffer et al. 2023, Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?. Quotes are exact. Fresh web check (July 2026): the "data wall" (Ilya Sutskever, 2024) and the still-open emergence argument.

Three things you can make bigger, and one number they move

Everything here is about a simple cause and effect. On one side, three things you can pour in more of. On the other, one number that says how good the machine is.

The three things you can make bigger (the field calls them the three ways to scale):

  • Size — how many adjustable numbers are inside the machine. These inner numbers are the "knobs" that training sets; more of them means a bigger machine. (The proper name is parameters.) Counted in billions.
  • Data — how much text you train on. (Counted in tokens — a token is a chunk of text, about a short word or a piece of a word.) More data means more to read. Counted in trillions of tokens.
  • Computer power — how much number-crunching you spend on training. (The proper name is compute, measured in FLOPs — the count of tiny arithmetic steps, like single multiplications. It is just a way to measure "how much calculating," the way metres measure distance.) More of it means a longer, heavier training run.

The one number they move:

  • The mistake-count. This is the score from rung next-word: how often, and how badly, the machine guesses the next word wrong. Lower is better. (Its proper name is the loss.) Everything below is the story of what happens to this one number as you turn up the three things above.

The big finding: a straight, steady line

Here is the discovery, in the exact words of the paper that found it. Read it once, then we unpack it:

"The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude." (Kaplan et al., "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models," 2020)

Two phrases to unpack, simply.

"Scales as a power-law." A power law here means a very steady rule: every time you multiply the size (or data, or compute) by the same amount, the mistakes drop by the same fraction. For example, make the machine 10 times bigger and the mistakes fall by a fixed slice. Make it 10 times bigger again, and they fall by the same-sized slice again. It is smooth and regular — no jumps, no luck.

There is a neat way to see this: if you draw the picture on a special chart where each step means "times 10" (instead of "plus 1") on both directions, the steady rule shows up as a perfectly straight line. That straight line is the most famous picture in modern AI.

"Seven orders of magnitude." An order of magnitude is just a factor of 10. Seven of them is ten million (10 × 10, seven times). So the straight line held true from tiny machines all the way up to machines ten million times larger. That is the shocking part. Not that bigger is better — everyone guessed that. The shock is that bigger is better so regularly that you can draw it with a ruler and read the future off it.

Why this one line changed the whole field

Think about what a straight, steady line lets you do. If you measure the mistakes for small and medium machines, you can extend the line and read off how good a giant machine will be — before you spend the millions of dollars to build it. The paper says exactly this:

"These relationships allow us to determine the optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget." (Kaplan et al., 2020)

("Optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget" = the best way to spend a set amount of computer power.) This turned a gamble into a plan. Instead of hoping a bigger machine would be better, labs could calculate it: pick a budget, predict the result, build the machine. That is why the whole field started making things bigger and bigger. [Established] — this steady line is one of the most re-tested results in AI.

What the line does NOT promise: it does not promise zero mistakes. The line falls toward a floor it can never go below. Why is there a floor? Because language has real, built-in surprise — the exact next word is often a genuine coin-flip that no machine, however large, can get right every time. Making the machine bigger closes the gap down to that floor, but never past it. [Established]

Chinchilla: the same money, spent smarter

The first finding said "make it bigger." But it did not clearly say how to split your money between the two costly things: more size, or more data? For about two years the field guessed wrong. A 2022 study caught the mistake:

"we find that current large language models are significantly undertrained ... for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled." (Hoffmann et al., "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models," 2022 — the "Chinchilla" paper)

Unpack it. "Undertrained" means the giant machines of 2020–2021 were the wrong shape: too many inner parts for the small amount of text they read — big brains that had not read enough. The fix, called compute-optimal (getting the best score for a set amount of computer power): grow the size and the amount of text together, hand in hand. Double the size, double the text.

They proved it the expensive way. They built a machine called Chinchilla (70 billion parts) and set it against a bigger machine called Gopher (280 billion parts), using the same computer power — but Chinchilla read 4 times more text. The smaller, better-read machine won:

"Chinchilla uniformly and significantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B) ... on a large range of downstream evaluation tasks." (Hoffmann et al., 2022)

The lasting lesson (which outlives the exact numbers): a bigger machine is not automatically a better machine. For a set budget there is a right shape, and for two years the field was building the wrong shape — too big, too little-read.

A newer twist (July 2026): Chinchilla answers "cheapest to train." But a machine is trained once and then run billions of times to answer people — and a bigger machine is more expensive to run every single time. So today labs often do the opposite on purpose: they take a smaller machine and train it on far more text than Chinchilla says — paying more up front to get a machine that is cheaper to run forever after. So do not memorise the "double for double" ratio; hold the real idea: balance training cost, running cost, and quality. The exact ratio changes; the trade-off stays. [Established]

The wall: there is only one internet

The steady line has a hidden catch, and it is now the biggest story in AI: the line needs you to keep feeding it more text. You cannot do that forever. This is the data wall.

The reason is simple. The Chinchilla rule says the amount of text must grow along with the size. But good human text — books, articles, good web pages, code — is a limited pile, and the biggest machines have already read a large part of all of it. The clearest warning came from Ilya Sutskever (a co-founder of the lab OpenAI) in a 2024 talk:

"Pre-training as we know it will unquestionably end ... because we have but one internet." (Ilya Sutskever, 2024; found on the web, July 2026)

("Pre-training" = the first, main training stage, where the machine reads huge amounts of text. "Unquestionably" = for sure.) He called data "the fossil fuel of AI" — like oil, the internet is a one-time supply built up over decades of human writing. You can burn through it fast, but you cannot make more original human text on demand. [Likely] as a near-term limit — people argue about when, not about the fact that text is finite.

What the field does now that the wall is here (July 2026)

Because there is not much new text left, the field's effort has moved off "just read more text" and onto other tricks — and this move is itself a sign that plain "make it bigger" is straining:

  • Make new text — have machines write their own training text, then keep only the good parts. This helps, but it has a known danger called model collapse (train a machine too much on its own writing, and the rare, unusual bits fade away — like a photocopy of a photocopy getting worse). So labs keep a lot of real human text and add machine-made text mostly for things that can be checked (math, code).
  • Polish after training — squeeze more out of a finished machine by extra shaping steps (teaching it to follow instructions, for example).
  • Think longer when answering — instead of a bigger machine, spend extra computer power at answer-time, letting the machine work step by step. This is a whole separate bet, with its own future page [AP2]. Experts now expect this answer-time computer power to grow larger than the training computer power by 2030.
  • Better training methods — smarter recipes are letting smaller machines catch up to bigger ones, showing that how you train is winning back ground from how big.

The plain summary: the steady line is not cancelled — it is running low on fuel. So gains now come from quality and cleverness, not raw size. Whether you call that "scaling is dead" or "scaling moved to new places" is exactly the argument on the AP1 page. [Contested] as a headline; [Established] that good human text is running short.

Emergence: skills that seem to switch on

Now the most argued idea on this page. The steady falling line is the predictable face of scale. But there is a stranger face. Some skills seem to be missing in smaller machines and then present in bigger ones — as if a switch flipped. The paper that named this:

"We consider an ability to be emergent if it is not present in smaller models but is present in larger models. Thus, emergent abilities cannot be predicted simply by extrapolating the performance of smaller models." (Wei et al., "Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models," 2022)

In plain words: an emergent skill is one you do not see in small machines, that suddenly appears in big ones — so you could not have guessed it was coming by watching the small ones. ("Extrapolating" = extending the pattern from smaller machines.) The examples included doing multi-step math, and answering in languages the machine barely saw.

Why did this shake people? Because it broke the comfort of the steady line. If new skills can appear with no warning at some unknown size, then you cannot fully know what your next, bigger machine will be able to do — including things you did not want it to do. That is a real safety worry. [Established as a thing that happens] — that test scores can jump sharply is not in doubt. What the jump means is very much in doubt.

The pushback: it may be a trick of the scoring

Here is the twist that makes this a real fight. A 2023 study argued that the "sudden switch" is often not a real change in the machine — it is caused by how we score the test:

"emergent abilities appear due [to] the researcher's choice of metric rather than due to fundamental changes in model behavior with scale ... alleged emergent abilities evaporate with different metrics or with better statistics." (Schaeffer, Miranda & Koyejo, "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?", 2023)

("Metric" = the way you score the test. "Evaporate" = disappear.) How can the score jump when the machine changed smoothly? Here is the trick, step by step — go slowly:

  1. Many tests use all-or-nothing scoring. Example: a multi-step math sum counts only if every digit is right. Get 4 of 5 digits right and you score zero.
  2. Under the surface, the machine's real skill — its chance of getting the whole thing right — is climbing smoothly as it grows, just like the steady line says.
  3. But the all-or-nothing score hides that smooth climb, showing "zero" for a long time, until the machine crosses the point where it usually gets the whole sum right. Only then does the score leap from near-0 to high.
  4. So the score jumped, but the skill rose smoothly the whole time. Switch to a fairer, part-marks score (count how many digits are right) and the "sudden jump" turns into a smooth slope.

Name the mistake clearly: a jump in the scoreboard was mistaken for a jump in the machine. The machine changed smoothly; the ruler was the jumpy part.

Where the fight stands (July 2026)

Do not tidy this into a winner — being honest is the point. The argument is still open. The scoring-trick idea is now widely accepted for many cases: a lot of "sudden skill" charts do smooth out under fairer scoring. But later work finds that a few sharp jumps survive even with fair scoring, and suggests these are real, sudden shifts that happen during training (like water turning to ice at 0°C — a sudden change of state at a threshold). The fair summary: "emergence" was over-sold as magic, but it was not entirely made up. So treat any single "skill X appeared at size Y" claim with care until you know how the test was scored. [Contested — open question]

⚠️ Honesty box

Scaling attracts two opposite exaggerations — "the line goes up forever, so AGI is just more computers" and "the line is a trick, so none of it is real." Both are wrong.

  • The line is real, but it measures mistakes, not wisdom. Fewer word-guessing mistakes is measured and solid, and it keeps falling as you scale. But "fewer mistakes" is not the same as "understands the world." Whether one becomes the other is a separate, open question — not settled by this line. [Established → Contested]
  • Extending the line is a bet, not a measurement. A straight line so far does not promise it stays straight. The line already bends toward its floor, and the data wall takes away the fuel it assumed. Reading "AGI" off a stretched-out line is a hope, not a proof. [Contested]
  • "Best shape" keeps changing. Chinchilla's neat rule was right for its question (cheapest to train) and already changed for a different question (cheapest to run). Any exact ratio you memorise will be out of date in a year; keep the trade-off, not the number. [Established]
  • "Emergent" is a word doing too much work. Some jumps are scoring tricks; some may be real sudden shifts; the word "emergent" quietly adds a feeling of magic that the evidence does not fully support. Keep the fact (scores can jump) apart from the story (a new skill switched on). [Contested]
  • Numbers age fast. "Ran out of data," "answer-time computer power grows past training by 2030," and any size figures are snapshots from 2020–2026. The lasting parts are the steady-line shape and the limit of human text; the numbers around them change quickly.

How to use this (if you want to direct AI work)

  • Ask which of the three things moved. When someone says a machine got better, ask: more size, more (or cleaner) text, more training power, or more answer-time thinking? The answer tells you whether the gain will keep coming or was a one-off. It is the closest thing to an X-ray of AI progress.
  • Treat the data wall as a strategy fact. If plain scaling is running low on text, the edge moves to better data, machine-made data, polishing, and answer-time thinking — that is where the returns are in 2026. Chasing "just make it bigger" is chasing a fuel that is running out.
  • Never trust an "it suddenly can do X" headline on its own. Ask: how was the test scored? All-or-nothing scoring invents fake cliffs; part-marks scoring often shows a smooth slope. That one question deflates most hype.
  • Keep training cost and running cost apart. The cheapest machine to build is rarely the cheapest to run. For a real product you usually want a smaller, over-trained machine.

Connections

  • Keep only three things: ① make a language model bigger and its mistakes fall in a steady, straight line you can predict far in advance; ② for a set budget there is a right shape (grow size and text together) — but human text is limited, so the line is now hitting a data wall; ③ skills that seem to "switch on" at large size are partly real and partly a scoring trick — the fight is not settled, so always ask how the test was scored.
  • Down the ladder (already read): guessing the next word — the "mistake-count" and why guessing forces real knowledge.
  • Up the ladder (next): AP1 · the "make it bigger" bet — this steady line is the whole reason people believe that bet.
  • How sure are we? The steady line and the limit of good text — [Established]. "Scaling alone reaches AGI" — [Contested → AP1]. "Sudden skills are real vs. a scoring trick" — [Contested, open]. Exact best-shape ratios — [out of date, now depends on running cost too].

Check yourself (try one, from memory)

  1. A friend says "they doubled the machine's size and the mistakes barely fell — scaling must be broken." Give two innocent reasons (use the words steady line and floor) before deciding anything is broken.
  2. Explain why Chinchilla — a smaller machine — beat a bigger one on the same computer power. Then explain why, even so, a company might train an even smaller machine on even more text.
  3. Say what the data wall is in one sentence, and name two things the field does once it hits the wall.
  4. A test shows a machine jump from 2% to 60% between two sizes. Give the "scoring trick" reason this jump might be fake — and then say honestly what part of the worry still stands.

Revision notes

Newest first.

  • rev 2 (2026-07-14) — rewritten to the simplest-English + progressive-ladder standard (HARD_RULES §6.5): short plain sentences, no fancy words, every term glossed. Now placed as rung 2 of the ladder, building on next-word with a short reminder-and-link (the "mistake-count" idea is owned there, not re-taught here). Same facts and quotes as rev 1; only the language and the ladder-wiring changed.
  • rev 1 (2026-07-14) — created as the mechanism page the AP1 bet pulls in. Grounded in the scaling papers (Kaplan, Chinchilla, Wei, Schaeffer); quotes exact; live-web freshness pass for the data wall and the open emergence argument.
